reading.synopsis: Verne Haskel, exhausted and embittered after twenty resentful years at Larson's Pump and Valve Works, retreats each evening to his basement, where he has spent his entire life building an obsessively exact miniature model of his hometown of Woodland — every store, house and street, down to the display cases in the shop windows. After a bad day, he tears the model of Larson's plant off the table and replaces it with a mortuary, then feels an intoxicating rush of power at how easily he erased it. He quits his job that afternoon and returns to systematically rebuild the entire town according to his grievances and preferences: destroying the homes and businesses of everyone who ever slighted him, rewarding those he favors, cleaning up the poor district, taming the rich one, and finally lettering his own name onto a Parthenon-styled city hall as its mayor. His wife Madge and her lover, psychiatrist Paul Tyler — who have been having an affair in the house while Haskel works below — first mock his hobby, then grow alarmed as Tyler recognizes buildings in the model that do not exist in the real Woodland, and finally, once Haskel declares himself finished and vanishes from the basement along with the model itself, decide the disappearance solves their problem and drive off to report him missing. On the way to the police station they pass, in the real town's darkness, the exact buildings Haskel invented — a mortuary and a pet shop that were never there before — moments before police cars box them in.

structure.form: short story in three movements: obsession established, escalation through vindictive redesign, confirmation that the model has become real
movements: The basement and the model as refuge: two decades of resentment against the town given physical, miniature form.
The destructive redesign, quitting his job, and Madge and Tyler's growing alarm as the model diverges from reality.
Completion, disappearance, and the couple's drive through a Woodland that has already begun to match the model — ending on their own arrest.
structure.point_of_view: third person, moving between Haskel's absorption in the basement and Madge and Tyler's rising unease upstairs, so the reader watches the same transformation from both the believer's and the skeptics' side simultaneously.
structure.central_device: The model changes the town it depicts, rather than merely depicting it — realized gradually, first as an unnerving coincidence and then as an inescapable fact, in the same order the reader receives it.

characters.name: Verne Haskel
characters.note: A 'little guy' in Palmer's phrase, exhausted and resentful, whose fantasy of control over Woodland is total and, unusually for this kind of story, actually succeeds.

characters.name: Madge Haskel
characters.note: Conducts an affair in her own living room with contempt for her husband's hobby, and is the one who first calls his lifelong project 'disgusting.'

characters.name: Dr. Paul Tyler
characters.note: Delivers a smug, textbook analysis of trains as boyhood power-and-control symbols, then is the first to notice the model no longer matches the real town — his professional authority undone by his own eyes.

settings.name: Woodland
settings.note: An upper-middle-class San Francisco suburb Haskel has resented his whole life for never fitting into — reproduced, then overwritten, in his basement.

settings.name: The basement workshop
settings.note: Trains, transformers, and the plywood town — a private, absolute domain answerable to no one, in sharp contrast to the plant and the marriage above it.

settings.name: The rebuilt Woodland
settings.note: Cleaned slums, a tamed wealthy district, a Parthenon-styled city hall bearing Haskel's name as mayor — utopian by his own narrow, vindictive lights.

motifs: The model as an instrument of literal, not merely psychological, control over the world it depicts
Grievance accounting: every destroyed building keyed to a specific remembered slight — a lead quarter, a dog bite, a refused loan
Trains and models as the boyhood language of mastery, explicitly diagnosed within the story by its own psychiatrist character
A a rewritten world confirmed real by the same skeptical, professional witness who first mocked it
Escape treated by the people left behind as a solution to be welcomed rather than a crisis to be addressed
reading.significance: Palmer reads this story alongside 'Exhibit Piece' as two variations on an idea Dick's fiction rarely admits outright: that escape from reality can be not just understandable but genuinely successful, without narrative punishment. The story is also, on Palmer's reading, a covert allegory of authorship — Haskel builds and then edits a miniature world down to the smallest storefront exactly as a novelist would, and the story does not distance itself from the parallel; Dick, per Palmer, 'stands inside the fiction' rather than treating Haskel's delusion from safe extrapolative remove. What makes the ending unsettling rather than triumphant is that Madge and Tyler are punished for wanting Haskel gone, not because Haskel's escape was wrong, but because the town he escaped into is now the only one left, and they are caught inside its rewritten version of the law.
reading.closing_note: The two shiny police cars that box in Tyler's Buick are, presumably, also Haskel's — the story ends without saying so, leaving the reader to draw the only available conclusion.

distinctive_terms.label: Greek
distinctive_terms.note: Haskel's city hall, modeled after the Parthenon — his one aesthetic ideal made literal.

distinctive_terms.label: Reality
distinctive_terms.note: Tyler's own diagnostic word for what Haskel is failing to face, turned against him.

distinctive_terms.label: Light
distinctive_terms.note: The new Woodland's 'indirect lighting' and well-lit streets, an explicit correction to a childhood grievance about Elm Street.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: Palmer's authorship-allegory reading: Haskel as a creator of a miniature world, paralleling the author's own relationship to fiction
a model that does not merely represent the town but progressively replaces it
Madge and Tyler's affair conducted in the house while Haskel works below, and their casual decision to treat his disappearance as a convenience
Haskel's entire grievance system and his utopian rebuild are keyed to suburban social slights — clerks, dress shops, mansions, dogs

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: In 'Small Town' (1954, CS2), a bitter, unsuccessful 'little guy' pours all his spirit into the modelling of a miniature
evidence.reading: Palmer's opening characterization of Haskel, framing the story within his broader account of Dick's 1950s 'little guy' protagonists.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: 'dream' fiction is often shy about: a sense that escape can be good. Let the reality principle go hang. But take 'Small Town' and 'Exhibit Piece' together as variations on an idea, and we have not a dialectic or a resolved contradiction, but an instability.
evidence.reading: The central critical claim: this story is unusual in Dick's fiction for treating successful escape from reality as something other than punished or ironized, and Palmer pairs it directly with 'Exhibit Piece' as a matched case.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: it is easy to read 'Small Town' or, for instance, 'Pay for the Printer', as allegories of authorship (the author as creator of miniature worlds, or of 'prints')
evidence.reading: Directly links this story to 'Pay for the Printer' (also read in this project) under a shared authorship-allegory reading — the author as a maker of small worlds rather than a mere describer of a real one.

open_questions: Palmer's pairing with 'Exhibit Piece' is substantial but 'Exhibit Piece' has not yet been read in this project — reading it would let the pairing be tested directly rather than taken on Palmer's word.

The 'instability' Palmer describes (neither dialectic nor resolved contradiction) is a fairly technical claim stated briefly; the surrounding argument in his book would clarify exactly what work he thinks the pairing does.
No PKD commentary was found on this story specifically — worth checking Dick's introductions or story notes in later collections, since he was known to write brief notes on his early stories.
